data.title: Wall Street stocks in relief rally after heavy AI-related selloff
data.description: NEW YORK/LONDON, Nov 6 : Wall Street equities mostly rallied on Friday, reversing course after trillions of dollars of world stock market value was wiped out over fears that Democratic election victories this week would bring tighter US regulations for the AI industry. Benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were trading higher with technology, communication services and consumer discretionary stocks driving gains. The Dow edged lower on the day. All three indexes were on track for weekly losses following a brutal selloff in the prior session. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.08 per cent, the S&P 500 rose 0.71 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.4 per cent. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was up 4.2 per cent after slumping in its biggest one-day drop since April 2025. Nvidia rose 3 per cent, after suffering its worst day since January 2025, when the emergence of low-cost Chinese AI model DeepSeek hammered markets. Other heavyweight chipmakers, including AMD, Intel, and Micron Technology, were up between 5.5 per cent and 10 per cent, while Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were also up 2 per cent and 8 per cent respectively after losses earlier this week. "Most of the disruption of the AI buildout will not probably occur but it's just the uncertainty of the change in government from Republican-led to Democratic-led, not only at the federal level but the state, local levels," said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at Sparrow Capital Management. "That's causing some disruption in the expectations of investors... The volatility around elections or any political event, whether it be war or terrorist attack, is always going to disrupt the market." Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said on Thursday that the state — which already has a large share of US data centres — will introduce new laws to protect local communities from their further mass buildup. The jitters are hitting an AI trade already under pressure from fears that the massive cost of the data centres and other infrastructure will limit future returns, spurring margin calls and spooking retail investors and hedge funds alike. RIPPLE EFFECT The bounces were in stark contrast with market action in the rest of the world. Europe's STOXX 600 lost 1 per cent. In Asia, Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's KOSPI both slumped about 6 per cent. For the Nikkei — just like Wall Street the previous day — it was the biggest one-day drop since US President Donald Trump's "Liberation Day" trade tariff panic of April 2025. The MSCI All-World index fell 0.52 per cent while MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan lost 3 per cent. PAYROLLS BEAT FORECASTS US nonfarm payrolls, usually one of the most-focused on pieces of data, but largely overshadowed by the tech drama, showed a stronger-than-expected 165,000 pickup in jobs. An anticipated slowdown in annual wage growth to below 3 per cent for the first time in nearly 5-1/2 years did not materialise either as it came in at 3.1 per cent. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note ticked up to 4.85 per cent, having dropped to its lowest level since September 9 overnight. In currencies, the dollar rose against major currencies including the euro, yen and Swiss franc. It was up 0.52 per cent against the yen and rose 0.47 per cent against the Swiss franc. The euro was down 0.68 per cent against the dollar at $1.1142. Brent crude prices tiptoed back up towards $100 a barrel, but are still set for their biggest weekly drop since 2020 on hopes the midterms' results might prompt Trump to de-escalate the Iran war. Spot gold fell 0.48 per cent to $4,067.75.

data.title: USDA to launch AI tool to check crop production data after errors
data.description: CHICAGO, Nov 6 : The US Department of Agriculture will use an artificial intelligence tool it built to check data in next week's monthly crop production report, agency officials said, after a series of data missteps eroded farmers' and traders' trust in its forecasts. After the USDA discovered errors in its corn data from September, officials determined the AI tool would have flagged the problem and decided to use it on the crop production report due on November 10, USDA Under Secretary Scott Hutchins said in an interview. The tool's debut tests whether the agency can restore confidence in data that often moves markets.  "I'm very bullish on the fact that we'll be able to utilize these tools in the future to help us avoid these kinds of really, truly unfortunate errors," Hutchins said on Thursday. Last month, the USDA corrected its September corn production and yield data. The correction raised the yield estimate by about 3 per cent in Nebraska, the third-biggest corn-producing state, and lowered it by about 2 per cent in Kansas.  The agency, long viewed as the gold standard of global agricultural market information, previously faced criticism after it made sharp upward revisions to estimates for last year's corn acreage. Over the summer, it  reported inaccurate beef export sales data. The USDA previously said it was launching a pilot project that would rely more heavily on technology to improve crop acreage and yield estimates as fewer farmers respond to its surveys.  COMPUTER FILE ERROR  Lance Honig, chair of the agricultural statistics board for USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service, told Reuters that a computer file incorrectly combined data on irrigated and non-irrigated corn acres gathered by field surveyors, causing the errors in September's data. Kansas and Nebraska were affected because they have higher percentages of irrigated fields, which often have higher yields, he said.  "This error that occurred in September is literally a very isolated occurrence that, quite frankly, with the proper validation, we should have caught," Honig said. "There was no issue with the data that was gathered at the field level." The errors angered farmers who are struggling to make money as they pay soaring prices for diesel, fertilizer and other inputs. Last month, the National Corn Growers Association, which represents 35,000 farmers, said the September errors were unacceptable and had further hurt farmers' confidence in the USDA's ability to produce accurate reports. "You just don't know what the USDA is going to do anymore," said Jim Gerlach, president of brokerage A/C Trading in Indiana, on Friday. "Their reports have become so erratic." Questions around the credibility of federal data increased after President Donald Trump's administration sharply downsized the government last year. Thousands of employees at the USDA have left, and experts have worried the cuts hobbled the agency's ability to produce accurate and timely data. Hutchins said the September errors were not related to staffing losses. The new AI tool will add to, not replace, the agency's data validation, he said.  "The tool is basically going to be used as a check to make sure that there are no anomalies that we were not able to see or identify in the normal process," Hutchins said.       This week, market analysts questioned the accuracy of another monthly USDA report on soy processing which showed a sharp divide between how many soybeans were crushed and how much soymeal was produced in Iowa.  The USDA said it was reviewing the report as part of a normal process and would make any necessary revisions next month.

data.title: OpenAI to press ahead with data-center expansion despite midterm sweep, CFO tells CNBC
data.description: Nov 6 : OpenAI will press ahead with its US data-center expansion plans despite a Democratic midterm sweep this week that has fueled fears of tighter scrutiny of the facilities, its Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar told CNBC in an interview on Friday. "When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet customer demand," Friar said. "We are going to keep building out those relationships with communities so we can get the compute we need," she added.  One of the corporate faces of the AI boom, OpenAI has moved quickly to counter fears that a shift in congressional power could slow the industry's growth. It launched a charm offensive on Thursday to win over communities as opposition to data centers becomes a rallying point for anxieties about the technology. As part of the efforts, OpenAI said, it will no longer use non-disclosure agreements with public officials when negotiating or discussing future sites. It will also give residents access to construction plans ⁠and their potential effects. Growing data-center opposition was a crucial issue in the midterm elections. Democratic candidates, including Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, made tighter scrutiny of the facilities a central campaign pledge. The Lone Star State is one of the fastest-growing data-center regions in the world. Fears the Democratic sweep may slow construction of the facilities critical to the AI boom wiped about $2.5 trillion off the US stock market on Thursday, as investors weighed the fallout for the chip, cloud and networking industries that have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the spending frenzy. Still, there are signs that tech giants remain committed to data-center expansion plans despite the growing backlash. Alphabet-owned Google said on Thursday it would invest $17 billion to build its first data center in Wyoming. Meanwhile, Bloomberg News reported that ByteDance is considering expanding a data center project in northeastern Brazil, a move that would strengthen its standing as Latin America's leading builder of computing facilities. OPENAI'S FUNDRAISING PLANS Friar also told CNBC that OpenAI was raising fresh capital, pushing back against suggestions the ChatGPT maker had scaled back its fundraising ambitions amid the sharp AI stocks selloff. The company is seeking fresh capital after its business grew 70 per cent quarter over quarter in the third quarter, with enterprise demand doubling over the same period, she said. "It (the growth) is saying people are actually using AI and getting value from it," Friar said. The fundraising comes as the market turmoil is raising questions about OpenAI rival Anthropic's widely awaited listing. Reuters reported on Thursday that prospective investors in Anthropic's IPO are questioning whether the AI startup can begin its roadshow next week and stay on track for a November listing. Investors are pushing ‌for a more attractive valuation to commit to the offering, with some viewing the recently discussed $1.5 trillion valuation as being at the high end of expectations, four people familiar with investor discussions told Reuters.

data.title: Nubank, Mercado Pago halt crypto transfers after external provider disruption
data.description: SAO PAULO, Nov 6 : Brazilian digital lender Nubank and Mercado Pago, the fintech arm from MercadoLibre, have halted some cryptocurrency transfers due to disruptions from an external data provider, the companies said in separate statements on Friday. • Nubank said it has halted cryptocurrency withdrawals and deposits • Mercado Pago said it blocked some transfers to external wallets, and added that deposits could also face delays • Both companies said client funds remain secure, and that other crypto products continue to operate as usual • Neither company identified the external provider involved, and it was unclear whether both were affected by the same provider • Nubank cited "instability from an external data provider," while Mercado Pago mentioned "an incident affecting a risk monitoring and anti-money laundering service provider" • Last week, hackers targeted exchange Binance to drain $6.3 billion worth of crypto, the largest such heist on record

data.title: Microsoft is winding down Oracle deal to rent AI cloud capacity, Bloomberg News reports
data.description: Nov 6 : Microsoft is winding down an arrangement to rent AI computing from Oracle as part of a larger reassessment of billions of dollars in cloud partnerships, Bloomberg News reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. Oracle shares were down nearly 3 per cent in afternoon trading, while Microsoft was little changed.  Microsoft has been turning off rented computing capacity from Oracle in recent months after declining to renew the contract, according to the report. Over time, the computing capacity Microsoft was renting became less valuable as it no longer met the company's evolving needs, the report added. Microsoft and Oracle did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

data.title: BOJ chief Ueda sees 'some upside risks' to inflation
data.description: WASHINGTON, Nov 6 : Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Friday the central bank expects underlying inflation to stay around its 2 per cent target but recognizes there are "some upside risks." The rise in prices of energy-related products was beginning to hit consumer inflation with price growth seen accelerating further into early next year, Ueda said. "We are in an equilibrium with wages growing at a level consistent with 2 per cent inflation," Ueda said at a seminar hosted by the International Monetary Fund. But the BOJ's 2 per cent inflation has yet to become a social norm in Japan, Ueda said, adding that the central bank's goal now was to anchor underlying inflation around its target. He also said the BOJ was looking at the actions of other central banks "very, very carefully," as they affect asset prices including foreign exchange rates and interest rates. "What they do reveals important information about what they think about their economies, which will impact our economy. So we look at their behavior and actions very carefully," he said on the policy measures of other central banks. On unconventional monetary policy tools, Ueda said they have had some positive effects when the BOJ deployed them, but added they have not been perfect substitutes for cutting interest rates from positive territory. The BOJ may be obliged to deploy unconventional policy tools again depending on the severity of the economic shock that may hit Japan, Ueda said. "I guess the important thing would be to keep inflation or underlying inflation at around 2 per cent as much as possible. But if we need to deploy these tools again, we should think about ways to minimize negative effects, including possibly the effect on the functioning of the market," he said.

data.title: Nubank halts crypto withdrawals, deposits after external provider disruption
data.description: SAO PAULO, Nov 6 : Brazilian digital lender Nubank said on Friday it has halted cryptocurrency withdrawals and deposits temporarily due to disruptions from an unnamed external data provider. • Nubank said the problem is not related to its own infrastructure and does not compromise customer security • All assets and information remain protected, the firm said • Operations will be resumed as soon as the service is restored, it added

data.title: BOJ's Ueda says Japan could do well with AI replacing labor, given existing shortages
data.description: WASHINGTON, Nov 6 : Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda on Friday said rapid advancements in artificial intelligence had provided a positive demand shock for the Japanese economy, but supply side factors would also need to be studied. Ueda, speaking at an event hosted by the International Monetary Fund, said Japan could do well with AI replacing labor given its significant labor shortages. He said he worried about cyber risks in terms of financial stability, adding that some small banks and small firms had not done enough to guard against such risks.

data.title: AI rout sets off market alarm signals as traders brace for what's next
data.description: LONDON, Nov 6 : A rout in technology stocks as confidence in the AI trade falters could test the resilience of global financial markets from New York to Taipei. The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 rose nearly 2 per cent on Friday, clawing back some of Thursday's more than 6 per cent plunge - but traders remain on edge. Policymakers have long warned of the risks from an AI boom unraveling. Investors and regulators are keeping a close watch on market stress indicators, with some flashing amber, although not yet red. Here's a look at how key measures are faring: FEAR IS UP Wall Street's fear gauge, the VIX index of US stock market volatility, rose to over 28 on Thursday, its highest since late March. It was holding close to that level on Friday. The increase is relatively contained compared to the post-April 2025 "Liberation Day" market jump and the August 2024 market selloff. Still, the VIX has surged more than 40 per cent this week. The European equivalent hit its highest level since May on Friday. "It's still early days," said Idanna Appio, a portfolio manager at First Eagle Investments. "My concern would be if we see more spikes in volatility, more stress, real issues with the ability to access markets. Those will be the things that...I'll be watching." PROTECTION FROM TECH TREMORS Perhaps the biggest harbinger of potential trouble in the AI space is a surge in insurance protection against a debt default. The cost of insuring debt issued by neocloud firm CoreWeave has spiked into distressed territory, with five-year credit default swap (CDS) spreads surging past 1,000 basis points to record highs. It has become a barometer of investor anxiety over AI. Spreads on credit default swaps for SpaceX and Intel have also jumped this week. The premium investors demand to hold US high yield corporate credit, known as junk bonds, has risen to its highest since the Liberation Day ructions as traders cool on riskier assets. In the riskiest parts of the market, for companies rated CCC or lower, that premium is trading at around its highest since 2020, according to ICE BofA indices. INVESTORS SEEK SAFETY A flight to safe havens is a clear sign of increased market angst, although daily moves are also relatively modest. US 10-year Treasury yields have fallen 50 bps from peaks above 5 per cent hit last month on concerns about high debt, rising inflation and competition for capital as tech firms ramped up bond sales. Currency markets were relatively muted, but there were some signs of investors seeking the US dollar, which was up 0.6 per cent as of 1500 GMT on Friday. Three-month euro cross-currency basis swaps, or the relative premium for swapping foreign currencies into dollars, briefly touched -8 bps on Thursday, the lowest since late 2023, signaling increased demand for dollar funding. It had recovered slightly on Friday to around -6 bps. BofA's Flow Show report on Friday said cash funds saw a $140 billion inflow in the week to Wednesday, the seventh biggest on record. BONDS BEHAVE Bond markets are so far showing no signs of the sort of stress they came under during the COVID-19 pandemic or around the Liberation Day tariffs. The closely watched MOVE index, which tracks volatility in the US Treasury market, hit a six-month high in October but has since slipped back. Other bond-market measures such as US swap spreads, which can indicate funding and liquidity stress, have also remained calm.

data.title: Trump administration scraps meeting of high-profile tech panel
data.description: WASHINGTON, Nov 6 : The Trump administration canceled a meeting on Friday of a White House tech panel that includes Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, an Energy Department spokesperson said. Technology shares sold off dramatically on Thursday on growing concerns that a new Congress controlled by Democrats will slow artificial intelligence development, and fears that the massive capital expenditure on building out AI will not yield sufficient returns. The market turmoil has heightened scrutiny of the sector among executives in Silicon Valley and policymakers in Washington. The meeting on Friday was scheduled to convene the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, an outside panel that advises President Donald Trump. The group also includes AMD CEO Lisa Su, Oracle Chief Technology Officer Larry Ellison and Marc Andreessen, the co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz. Its co-chairs are venture capitalist David Sacks and White House tech adviser Michael Kratsios. The Energy Department's meeting website briefly listed November 13 as the new date for the meeting, but the agency later sent an email retracting that.  The initial meeting announcement said the panel would advise Trump's new AI task force, dubbed the "Super Intelligence Task Force," which includes cabinet officials, Trump appointees and White House staff. Super intelligence is the president's preferred term for AI. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment about why the science and technology meeting was postponed.

data.title: TikTok owner ByteDance weighs data center expansion in Brazil, Bloomberg News reports
data.description: Nov 6 : TikTok owner ByteDance is considering expanding a data center project in northeastern Brazil, Bloomberg News reported on Friday.

data.title: Charter to cut $2 billion in costs under 'fundamental redesign' to revive growth
data.description: Nov 6 : Charter Communications said on Friday it would cut $2 billion in annualized operating costs over the next 18 months as part of an overhaul of its operating model aimed at reviving growth in a competitive cable and broadband market. Shares of the company fell more than 3 per cent in morning trading. They have fallen 39.7 per cent so far this year through Thursday's close. Charter said it would revamp how it markets and sells its core internet service and lean more on its mobile and video products to add customers and improve retention. Charter has "not generated the customer growth and performance we expect," CEO Chris Winfrey said on a post-earnings call. The cost cuts are separate from more than $1 billion in anticipated synergies from Charter's acquisition of Cox Communications, which closed on August 19. The $34.5 billion deal, including debt, combined two of the largest US cable and broadband operators as Netflix, Disney+, Verizon and T-Mobile intensify competition for customers. Charter lost 233,000 internet customers in the third quarter on a pro forma basis, versus a loss of 171,000 a year earlier, while video customers fell by 77,000, compared with a decline of 121,000. "Charter’s mounting broadband losses are alarming and underscore the scale of the challenge," said Paolo Pescatore, founder of PP Foresight. The $2 billion cost-cutting program is necessary, but "it cannot simply cut its way back to growth," he added. Charter on Friday reported third-quarter revenue of $14.9 billion, below analysts' average estimate of $15.03 billion, according to LSEG data.  It posted a net loss of $20.50 per share, versus income of $8.50 last year, driven mainly by a $6.3 billion franchise impairment charge. The company had total debt of $108.6 billion at the end of September, against cash of $573 million. Separately, Reuters reported on Tuesday India's Jio Platforms has held talks with Charter and Comcast about licensing its wireless broadband technology for potential stakes.

data.title: Firefly inks $1.3 billion deal to supply engines for new AST SpaceMobile 'Blacklift' rocket
data.description: WASHINGTON, Nov 6 : Firefly Aerospace will supply core engines for a new rocket under development by satellite communications firm AST SpaceMobile in a $1.3 billion deal, underscoring a push among satellite companies to secure dependable access to space. The engine deal, announced on Friday, is a key part of new plans by AST SpaceMobile to develop its own heavy-lift rocket named Blacklift as it races to deploy a satellite constellation for global cellular broadband service and wean itself off a reliance on third-party rockets like SpaceX's Falcon 9. Firefly will build and supply 27 of its new Miranda engines and 9 in-space Vira engines for the first three Blacklift rockets under the agreement, which also grants a license to AST to eventually manufacture the engines itself. AST said it is targeting late 2028 for the debut launch of Blacklift, an ambitious development timeline. The company said the rocket is "designed for reusability" and can loft up to five of its BlueBird satellites per launch.

data.title: Fox completes $22 billion Roku deal to expand digital reach
data.description: Nov 6 : Fox Corp on Friday completed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, a major bet that the streaming platform will bolster the broadcaster's advertising business and expand the online reach of its sports and news programming. Announced in June, the cash-and-stock deal gives Fox access to the more than 100 million households using Roku's platform, potentially helping the cable TV-reliant media company build a larger digital audience and better target ads.
